abstract: Human cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A), which catalyzes the hydrolysis of AMP to adenosine, is a prominent autoantigen in the progressive myopathy inclusion body myositis (IBM). Detection of anti-cN1A autoantibodies is a supportive criterion for IBM diagnosis, and mice immunized actively or passively with cN1A develop an IBM phenotype. However, how cN1A breaks immunotolerance is not yet known. Despite its clinical significance, the subcellular localization of cN1A is not well understood, and its structure has not been determined. Here, we show that human cN1A is most highly expressed in type 2 myofibers and tends to localize near the periphery of muscle fibers, but is either weakly expressed or undetectable in commonly used human cell lines. Ectopic expression of cN1A in such cells resulted in spontaneous assembly of cN1A into filamentous structures strikingly similar to metabolic filaments formed by the nucleotide biosynthesis enzymes IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH) and CTP synthase (CTPS). However, cN1A filaments did not co-localize with IMPDH or CTPS filaments and were not responsive to compounds that induce IMPDH and CTPS assembly. Negative stain electron microscopy (EM) showed that purified recombinant cN1A protein spontaneously polymerizes, suggesting filament assembly in cells is driven by intrinsic properties of cN1A. We then determined the structure of the cN1A filament by cryo-EM, which revealed that cN1A monomers assemble end-on-end into a polar helical filament and allowed us to identify contacts mediating filament assembly. Structure-guided mutations designed to abolish filament assembly prevented cN1A filament formation in cells, establishing the structural basis for cN1A filament assembly.
